mainEntity.name: Who is responsible for the fence between two homes in a Michigan subdivision?

acceptedAnswer.text: It depends on the recorded documents first and Michigan law second. If the fence sits on private property, the owner who built it pays for it under MCL 43.53, and an adjoining owner who uses it may owe a proportional share determined by a fence viewer. If the association's restrictions or master deed assign the fence to the association, the association pays.

mainEntity.name: Does a Michigan HOA have to approve my fence?

acceptedAnswer.text: Only if the recorded declaration, bylaws, or architectural guidelines give it that authority, which most do. The approval criteria should be written, applied consistently, and decided within a stated window. A city permit may also be required, and an association approval does not replace it.

mainEntity.name: Can my HOA make me remove a fence that was already there when I bought the house?

acceptedAnswer.text: Possibly, depending on the documents. Many declarations grandfather pre-existing fences until replacement, while others require compliance on any change of ownership or reconstruction. The board should be able to cite the specific provision, and the answer should be the same for every owner.

mainEntity.name: How much should an HOA budget for fence replacement?

acceptedAnswer.text: Budget from measurement, not from a rule of thumb. A six-foot board-on-board cedar run in Oakland County in 2026 runs roughly $55 to $70 per linear foot installed, including tear-out and disposal and excluding gates and staining. A 400-foot common run is therefore a $22,000 to $28,000 line item.

mainEntity.name: Is a fence a common element or a limited common element?

acceptedAnswer.text: It depends on the master deed and the condominium plan. A fence on common area is generally a general common element paid by the association. A fence reserved to specific units is a limited common element specially assessed to those units under MCL 559.169. In many site condominiums, the yard is part of the unit, which makes the fence private.

mainEntity.name: Can an HOA use reserve funds to replace a fence?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, if the fence is a common element being repaired or replaced and the documents permit it. Under MCL 559.205 and Mich Admin Code R 559.511, the reserve fund exists for major repair and replacement of common elements and must be at least 10% of the current annual budget, noncumulative. Using it for routine upkeep is not allowed.

mainEntity.name: How long does an HOA fence replacement take from approval to finished fence?

acceptedAnswer.text: Plan on four to six months. Bidding takes two to three weeks, contract and material ordering another four to eight weeks, permits vary by city, and construction of a 400-foot run with tear-out is typically three to five days of on-site work once the ground is workable.

mainEntity.name: What should be in an HOA fence bid package?

acceptedAnswer.text: Nine items: measured linear feet by run, height and style, post and rail specifications, species and grade, footing depth below frost, gate count and hardware, removal and disposal, finish specification, and insurance, permits, schedule, and warranty. Requiring all nine in writing is what makes three bids comparable.
